tweets.creator: @kilocode
tweets.text: The blocks physics simulator pushed the two models furthest apart. The prompt asked for draggable 3D blocks that stack and tumble when they are off balance. Auto Efficient built it for $0.05, and Opus built it for $1.31. That is 26 times the cost for the same prompt.

tweets.creator: @kilocode
tweets.text: Same prompt to both models: animate the Earth spinning in space. The clip shows both results side by side. Auto Efficient rendered it for one cent. Opus rendered it for 37 cents. Video

tweets.creator: @kilocode
tweets.text: Opus is the stronger model. It completed 67.6% of tasks to Auto Efficient's 46.7%. But here is the part that matters for your bill: Auto Efficient did it at 77% lower cost per attempt. $19.60 versus $85.19. That is 69% of Opus completion for less than a quarter of the cost.

tweets.creator: @kilocode
tweets.text: This is the case for routing per task instead of picking one model per seat. You set a tier. Kilo reads the session intent and sends each task to the right model based on benchmarks and live usage data, instead of whatever you guessed at config time.

tweets.creator: @kilocode
tweets.text: The thing that actually works: stop paying frontier prices for tasks that don't need a frontier model. Most coding work doesn't. A big chunk of real tasks land fine on an efficient model for a fraction of the cost.

tweets.creator: @kilocode
tweets.text: The usual reaction is to cap usage or move everyone to a cheaper model. Both of these quietly tax your team. Caps mean engineers sit and wait. Blanket downgrades mean worse output on the tasks that actually needed the good model.
